coach_says: Taking back with bxa5 gets the pawn back but leaves you with two weak, doubled a-pawns and opens the b-file for White: Rb1 and Rb7 put a rook on your seventh rank, hitting c7. First kick the rook with 22...c6, then win the pawn back with Rxa5, so your rook is the active one. Before recapturing, ask which files and pawns the recapture hands your opponent.
also: kick the rook first with c6

coach_says: Qf3 aims at f7, but Black has castled, so f7 is defended by both the king and the rook, and the attack goes nowhere. Worse, your queen now sits on f3, the square your g5 knight needs to retreat to. After ...h6 the knight can only go to h3 or sacrifice itself on f7, and ...Nd4 hits your queen and c2. Against a castled king, finish developing (Nc3, c3, castle) and bring the knight back before it gets stuck.
also: Nd4 hits the queen with tempo

coach_says: Taking with the bishop lets White trade it off with Nxd5 Nxd5, and then your knight on d5 has no defender and your queen on e7 is easy to hit. Bg5 forces ...f6, and Be4 then hits the d5 knight, so White wins material or wrecks your kingside. Take with the knight, 8...Nxd5: the bishop on e6 keeps guarding d5 and you stay solid. When two pieces can recapture, check what each one leaves loose.
also: Bg5 hits the queen on e7

coach_says: You're a pawn up and Black's rook on a8 is staring at yours on a1. Trade it yourself with Rxa8, so Black's queen doesn't get the a-file, then finish developing with Ne2, d3 and castling. f4 does nothing for your pieces and loosens g3 and e4, giving Black's h5 knight the g3 square. When you're ahead, develop and trade rather than make pawn moves.
also: trade rooks on the open a-file

coach_says: Your bishop was attacked, but you had a stronger move than retreating: 17. dxe5! clears the d-file, and the knight on d5 has no defender because d6 blocks Black's queen. If ...gxh4, Qxd5 wins the knight, so Black has to deal with that and you save the bishop next move. After Bg3, Black gets ...e4, hitting your f3 knight and gaining space. When a piece is attacked, look for a forcing move first that creates a bigger threat.
also: pawn push e4 hits the knight

coach_says: Your bishop on c1 was the only piece guarding b2. When it goes to f4, Qxb2 takes a pawn and hits your knight on c3, which nothing defends any more, and your rook on a1. Black's bishop on d4 is also aiming at c3. Be3 was the move: it offers to trade off Black's strong d4 bishop and keeps b2 covered. Before moving a piece, check what it was defending.

Black's d5 pawn attacks your e4 pawn. The simple answer is to take it, 2. exd5, and if the queen recaptures you develop with Nc3 and gain time against it. 2. f3 guards e4 but takes the f3 square from your knight and opens the diagonal to your king, so ...e5 and ...Bc5 point straight at g1. In the opening, meet a central pawn challenge by capturing or developing, not by pushing the f-pawn.

Your d5 pawn is attacked by c4 and e4, and White's only guard of c4 is the d3 pawn. 7...dxe4! pulls that guard away: after 8. dxe4 you take on c4 with the bishop and win a pawn. Bb4 ignores the tension, White plays exd5 cxd5, and your centre becomes a target for d4. When pawns are in contact, look at what each capture wins or opens before developing elsewhere.

Before taking back on e5, look at your d5 pawn: the c3 knight attacks it and nothing guards it. After fxe5, Nxd5 wins it and opens lines towards your king, which is still in the centre with a loose kingside. 12...g4 first attacks the f3 knight, so if White takes on d5 you take the knight. When you recapture, check every attacked pawn and piece of yours first.

In the Advance Caro-Kann, the plan is 3...Bf5: get your light-squared bishop out before ...e6 locks it in. 3...f5 takes that square from your bishop and leaves a permanent hole on e6 and a backward e-pawn. White can open the centre with c4 and use those light squares. Develop the bishop first, then play ...e6.
2. c4 is a perfectly good move. It takes space and keeps d4 and e4 for later. Carry on developing.

Good move. White was threatening Bxc6 and Nxe5 to win your e5 pawn, and Nge7 defends c6 so that trick no longer works. Next, keep your king safe from checks on the d-file and develop the rest of your pieces.
Bb4 is fine. It pins the c3 knight. Watch out for Qb3, which hits b7, and be ready to defend it with ...Nc6 and ...Rb8 or by trading on c3.
2. Bc4 is playable, though against the Sicilian the bishop often hits a wall once Black plays ...e6 and ...d5. Nf3 then d4 is the more natural plan, but this isn't a mistake.
Your bishop was attacked and you retreated it to a safe square, which is fine. Taking on d2 or retreating to d6 was about as good. The bishop on e7 is a bit passive, but it's not a mistake.

a5 is one of the best moves. It pushes your queenside majority towards making a passed pawn while your king and bishop support it. Keep going: bring the king up with Kc4 and use b4 and b5 to break through.

Qg3+ is the best move. You keep checking and then pick up the f3 pawn with check, which keeps White's queen too busy to go after your d6 pawn. Keep the checks going until you can win more pawns or push your h-pawn.
Kb7 is fine. Your king heads for a7 to win the last black pawn and then escort your a-pawn. Giving up f4 doesn't matter, because Black's king is too far away to stop your queenside pawn for long.
Qe7 is reasonable. It defends e5 and gets ready to castle queenside. It does block your f8 bishop for now. Moves like ...Rg8 to use the open g-file were a little better, but the difference is small.

Excellent. Bb5+ forces ...c6, and Qxd5 then wins a knight, because the c6 pawn is pinned to your king by the bishop and cannot take back. Pinning a defender with check is worth looking for every move.
